data: Coarse-grained, banded, white marble, likely Proconnesian. Digital microscopy: heteroblastic fabric (identification based on pXRF, digital microscopy)

Five lines of Latin text, in straight alignment and shifted toward the right, with a wider left margin.The letters in the first line, which is partially legible, are of slightly greater module than those in the following lines, and are more widely spaced. The last line – of which only parts of one or more letters are preserved (perhaps an A and and the left apex of a V; an M is also possible) are preserved – appears more centered, with both left and right margins wider.

Elegant square capital letters, slightly verticalized, with serifs. The O in l. 1 is square in shape compared to the O in the other lines; A has a vertical crossbar, P has an open loop. In l. 2, a triple nexus links the letters T, R, and I, with the I rising above. In l. 4, there is spacing between the words Sosius and Priscus. Comma-shaped punctuation marks appear in ll. 1 and 3. A damaged ivy leaf appears at the end of l. 1.
Early 2nd century, mother of cos. 108 CE

Lettering of this sort can be observed already in the later Hellenistic period in Sicily, but the use of marble may suggest that the piece belongs in the Roman period, although the absence of Roman names in turn might suggest an earlier date. Perhaps second century CE?

Five lines of Greek text, with a regular left margin, but uneven right margin; line 3 in particular shows signs of cramping in the second half. The lower half of the final line is lost through damage.

Neat, regular letters, mostly of wide module, without serifs. Alpha is broad with straight bar; epsilon has notably short middle bar; kappa has arms of almost full length; omicron is only lightly smaller than other letters (19-20 mm); pi has even length vertical hastae; rho has small closed round head; sigma is four bar with extended horizontal top and bottom strokes; upsilon is neatly symmetrical; phi has small circular eye with vertical only slightly extended (26 mm); omega is full-size and nearly circular, closed, with long horizontal.
later Hellenistic (i.e. 2nd or early 1st century BCE)
